text: Robert Adams (5 October 1917 – 5 April 1984) was an English sculptor and designer who, though not widely known outside artistic circles, was regarded as one of the foremost sculptors of his generation. In a 1993 retrospective review by Brian Glasser of Time Out magazine, Adams was described as "the neglected genius of post-war British sculpture," a view also expressed by Tim Hilton in the Sunday Independent, who ranked his work above that of contemporaries Ken Armitage, Reg Butler, Lynn Chadwick, and Bernard Meadows. Adams attended the village school in Hardingstone, Northamptonshire, now a suburb of Northampton, and lived there until 1951. He left school at age 14 and worked in various manual jobs, first as a van-boy for a printer and later with the agricultural engineering company Cooch & Sons, where experience in metal crafting proved valuable in his later art. From 1937 to 1946, he attended evening classes in life drawing and painting at the Northampton School of Art. During the Second World War, Adams was a conscientious objector but joined the Civil Defence as a fire warden. Some of his early sculptures were exhibited in London between 1942 and 1944 in group shows by Civil Defence artists. In April 1946, he exhibited fourteen early oil portraits at the Northampton Public Library. Between 23 November 1947 and 3 January 1948, he held his first one-man exhibition at Gimpel Fils Gallery, 84 Duke Street, London. From 1949 to 1959, he taught at the Central School of Art and Design in London, where he interacted with Victor Pasmore, Kenneth Martin, and Mary Martin, who were advancing Constructivist ideas in Britain. From 1950 to 1980, he was recognized as one of Britain's leading abstract sculptors, with his work exhibited at the Venice Biennale in 1952 and again in 1962 when he represented Britain with a retrospective in two galleries. Some of his works are held in the Tate Britain collection and in modern art museums in New York, Rome, Turin, São Paulo, and several other global locations, though he remains virtually unknown in his hometown. The Apocalyptic Figure was commissioned by the Arts Council England for the Festival of Britain in 1951. Large-scale sculptures by Adams can be seen at The Custom House, London, Heathrow Airport, Shell Mex House, London, and the Musiktheater im Revier, Gelsenkirchen, Germany, and one of his works is in the Contemporary Art Museum of Macedonia. He also had a retrospective at the Northampton Art Gallery in 1971.
